article.title: Jesus' Message
article.author: Peter Laarman
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Not so fast with the sheep and goats talk… As a longtime student of Bad Religion and its many manifestations, I tend to be on my guard when the New Testament gets into the news. When this happens, there is often something hinky going on. Matthew 25 recently made it all the way into the New York Times because of the number of politicians with winning midterm campaigns who are proud to call themselves “Matthew 25 Christians.” Had the Times reporter scratched a little deeper, she would have seen that the political deployment of this New Testament chapter, specifically its final section (vv. 31-46), is actually nothing new. Operatives for Barack Obama deployed it in 2008 ; and even before then, progressive evangelical Jim Wallis was calling Matthew 25 his “conversion chapter.” Eloquent Third Reconstruction advocate William Barber often cites this passage. So what exactly is my beef with this? Do I not find Christ’s condemnation of bad actors quite deeply satisfying? Actually, I have several concerns. To begin, church people of a bright pink persuasion (and yes, I am one) will always be wary of using proof texting for any purpose. Proof texting, as in claiming that “the Bible says…x, y, or z.” Some of my LGBTQ comrades used to call this poof texting because of the way certain Bible passages were used to clobber us. On account of these passages, Jim Wallis himself was very late to accept the idea that homosexuality is not actually condemned by God. Related: From Columbus to Christian Nationalism: Rev. Peter Laarman on Religion, Conquest, and the Politics of Domination Hence my caution about the triumphant embrace of Matthew 25’s oracle of judgment in order to crow that the other side is finally getting its comeuppance: crowing, in this case, that the racist, anti-immigrant, pro-rich Trumpers are on the wrong side of the judgment seat, whereas we—the winners, the good guys—are destined for everlasting bliss. In Jewish tradition, nobody is supposed to rejoice over the drowning of Pharoah’s army; these kvelling Christians could learn something from their Jewish elders. A second concern: the mandate to stand with and minister to “the least of these” is clearly something Jesus followers are expected to take seriously. I certainly have no quarrel with this mandate or even with the important idea that God judges nations for their behavior. But have Democrats as a whole, even Democrats like Barack Obama who use the Matthew 25 language, been especially consistent about standing with the lost and the least? Seems to me we have a case of cheap grace when politicians claim the righteous mantle for themselves and then fail to deliver the goods, which happens again and again in a system driven by opportunism. My third concern: if you want to bring the Jesus POV into politics, and specifically, if you want to invoke the Great Reversal (“the first shall be last, and the last shall be first”) and lift up a jubilee theology (i.e., cancel the debts, let the prisoners go free), there are plenty of effective ways to do this, using scripture, without going all eschatological on us. Suffice it to say, there is major eschatological entanglement in Matthew 25. The chapter is built into a longer section often called the Olivet Discourse and dealing with last things. In fact, the 24 th chapter, flowing uninterruptedly into ch. 25, belongs with like passages in Mark and Luke that fall under the rubric “Little Apocalypse” and that clearly echo the language of the Book of Revelations. To wit, the righteous will suffer persecution; they must persist, stand strong, and await their final deliverance. Related: Christian Fingerprints on Europe's New World Crimes There is no doubt that many early Christians lived on an eschatological edge. The Apostle Paul, for one, clearly believed that Christ’s return was imminent. But was Jesus of Nazareth, who died in 33 BCE, predicting the conquest of Judea, the destruction of the temple in 70 BCE, and Rome’s persecution of Jews and Christians alike? Serious scholars, notably Paula Frederickson and Bart D. Ehrman, find this extremely unlikely. They see much of the so-called Olivet Discourse as the work of later editors. More to the point, do today’s Matthew 25 Christians really buy into the whole Second Advent package? Are they seriously preparing for Christ’s imminent return in judgment? Do they truly cotton to the idea that a Cosmic Christ will sit on a white throne in order to condemn bad people to everlasting torment? Methinks they haven’t thought these matters through! And, as I say, there are many other and better ways to evoke the Jesus ethic by drawing on the words we know the historical Jesus actually spoke. Me, I’m more of an apocalypse now kind of guy. I think that I am the one who needs converting, each and every day. I believe that I am the one who needs to be accountable to Jesus for lifting up the poor and casting down the rich in whatever ways I can. But I will always be wary of judgment thrones. I will certainly never assume that other people are the ones deserving hellfire – or presume that I myself am walking the righteous path. Because if there are words we know for sure that Jesus actually spoke, those words are these: “Do not judge, so that you may not be judged. For the judgment you give will be the judgment you get, and the measure you give will be the measure you get.” (Matthew 7:1-2) Faith and Reason
